166:
Where the conservatives came from

Li Xun argues that in many factories and schools, the first split between rebels and conservatives came from how people stood toward the work teams and the Party committees. In summer 1966, Party committees and work teams at every level singled out experts, scholars, and people of “bad class background” as targets of the movement. Anyone who put up a big-character poster questioning the Party committee itself was at once mobbed by crowds the committee had mobilized. Most of the critics who were mobbed later became rebels. Many of those who followed the Party committees and work teams into the mobbing later became the core of the conservative organizations. Wang Hongwen's experience at No. 17 Mill was of the first kind. History See Li Xun, “A Neglected History: Taking the Study of Cultural Revolution Conservatives Seriously” (《被忽略的历史：重视对文革保守派的研究》).

The conservatives became truly active after September 1966. In late August and early September, Beijing Red Guards stormed the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee, and many workers went to its gates to “defend the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee.” The two most famous big-character posters were “We Old Workers Must Speak,” written in the name of veteran workers at No. 2 State Cotton Mill, and “Urgent Telegram to Chairman Mao,” written in the name of the model worker Yang Fuzhen. It later came out that the first was drafted by the secretary of the mill's Party committee, and the second by the Municipal Party Committee work team stationed in the mill, with Chen Pixian's approval. The workers who went to argue at the gates had been sent by their factory Party committees at the Municipal Party Committee's request. All of it counted as official leave. The cadres who organized them told them, if anyone asks, say you came on your own. History See Li Xun, “A Neglected History: Taking the Study of Cultural Revolution Conservatives Seriously” (《被忽略的历史：重视对文革保守派的研究》). Li Xun was herself a conservative middle school student in Shanghai at the time.

Li Xun calls this a continuation of the mobilization model of seventeen years of political campaigns. From the Anti-Rightist Campaign of 1957 to 1966, “speaking in the name of the workers” happened again and again. Interpretation
167:
The bureau's work team stayed only a month. On July 20, the Municipal Party Committee sent a new one, about 150 people, led by Shi Huizhen, Vice Chairman of the city's trade union federation. The bureau's team pulled out the next day. They did not say goodbye to you when they left.

You heard the new work team's report three times, and each time it sat less right with you. The report said the focus of the movement was to “hunt down all ox-demons and snake-spirits.” It called on every worker in the mill to “search for tigers in the deep mountains and dense forests.” The things you had exposed were not mentioned once.

Who were the tigers? Talk started in the workshops. The people who had put up the big-character poster, it was said, all had problems in their past.

A colleague in the security section told you something. He said it in a low voice. The work team was collecting material. Who put up which big-character poster, who said what at meetings, who was close to whom. All of it was written down, item by item, and put into dossiers.

You had worked in the security section for six years. You knew better than anyone what a dossier meant. Those few pages follow a person for life. Every transfer, every Party application, every promotion, every housing assignment, they get pulled out and read. And the person never gets to see what is written in them.

In August the papers printed the Sixteen Points. You read it through in the canteen, slapped the table, and said, “It's as if the Center is pointing straight at the situation in our mill.” The Sixteen Points said the focus of the movement was to rectify those Party persons in power taking the capitalist road, and to guard against anyone branding the masses as counterrevolutionaries.

But in the mill, nothing changed.

In early September, Red Guards from Beijing stormed the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee. The mill sent a truckload of people to West Yan'an Road to “defend the Municipal Party Committee.” It counted as official leave. When they came back they said the cadres who organized it had told them, if anyone asks, say you came on your own. The gates of the Municipal Party Committee were covered in big-character posters. One was called “We Old Workers Must Speak.” It was copied out as a leaflet, and everyone in the mill got one. Later another leaflet said that poster had been drafted by the secretary of the No. 2 State Cotton Mill Party committee.

The work team organized four mill-wide mass debates, and every one of them was about you and your group. At the one on October 10, a crowd surrounded you, pushing and shoving, and someone spat in your face. You remembered that face. He was a maintenance fitter from the spinning workshop who used to offer you a cigarette when you met. He had been on the truck to West Yan'an Road in September to defend the Municipal Party Committee. In all four debates, most of the people around you came from that truck.

In the end a group of students from the mill's vocational school burst in and pulled you out. The boy leading them was only eighteen. His name was Liao Zukang.
168: That night you did not sleep. You decided to go to Beijing.

171: Beijing · On the train back to Shanghai
173:
Several people pooled money for your train ticket to Beijing. In those days a worker who left his post could have his wages docked and get a disciplinary mark. Very few dared to do it.

Beijing and Shanghai were two different worlds. Red Guards filled the streets, and big-character posters covered every wall. You heard that the Center had just held a meeting and Red Flag had run an editorial criticizing the “bourgeois reactionary line.” Sending work teams to persecute the masses now had a name. It was called the reactionary line. People who had been persecuted could demand rehabilitation, and black materials were to be burned in public.

You queued for two days at the reception station and handed in a written account of the situation at No. 17 State Cotton Mill. No one wrote back. But you felt the wind had changed.

On the train back to Shanghai you kept thinking. The students in Beijing had risen. What about the workers in Shanghai?

On your third day back at the mill, Wang Xiuzhen of No. 30 State Cotton Mill sent someone to invite you over to tell her mill about the situation in Beijing. She was a model worker, and her factory Party committee had held her down too. On the fifth day, Huang Jinhai of No. 31 State Cotton Mill came to your mill himself to find you.

Huang Jinhai was a Five-Good Worker. In June he put up a big-character poster saying the Party general branch had the wrong attitude toward studying Mao's works. For that one sentence he was branded an anti-Party, anti-socialist element. His wife cried at home every day. The men who used to share his table in the canteen now picked up their lunch boxes and moved away. He took his complaint to the Municipal Party Committee. Nothing came of it.

When he told you all this his voice was flat, and he smoked the whole time. When he finished, he asked you, “So what are they really saying in Beijing?”

You realized there were people like you in every factory.

History In October Wang Hongwen went to Beijing to petition, with ticket money pooled by others. Very few workers dared to leave their posts at the time. After he returned to Shanghai, Wang Xiuzhen and then Huang Jinhai asked him to report on the situation in Beijing. See Li Xun, “The Era of Revolutionary Rebellion” (《革命造反年代》), ch. 6.

History Huang Jinhai was a Shanghai Five-Good Worker in 1965. In June he put up a big-character poster criticizing the Party general branch's attitude toward studying Mao's works and was branded an anti-Party, anti-socialist element. His wife wept at home, coworkers avoided him, and his complaint to the Municipal Party Committee went nowhere. See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), and the Wikipedia entry “Huang Jinhai.”

178:
You took the tram from Yangshupu and changed twice. It took over an hour. It was supposed to be a quick meeting, but more than a dozen people came, from more than a dozen factories, and most had met each other only once or twice. The room was thick with smoke. Even with the windows open it would not clear.

⟦0⟧

At first everyone took turns talking about their own factory. A man from the Shanghai Railway Bureau loading machinery plant said conservatives at his plant had set up their own kangaroo court and locked rebels up and beat them. Halfway through he could not go on, and the man next to him finished for him. Another said his factory Party committee had announced that anyone who put up another big-character poster would get no grade raise at year's end. A temporary worker said that as a temporary worker he had no dossier to begin with, and the factory could fire him whenever it liked. His surname was Fan, Fan Fulin. He kept rubbing his hands while he talked.

As they talked, the mood in the room changed. Alone in his own factory, each of them was the one being persecuted. Sitting together, they found they were a crowd.

Someone said, fighting one factory at a time, we'll never win. Above the Party committee there's the bureau, and above the bureau there's the Municipal Party Committee. We need a citywide organization, across factories, across industries.

Someone said, the Center never said workers could link up across factories. The Municipal Party Committee will never recognize it.

Pan Guoping, a young worker from the glass machinery plant, stood up. He was barely past twenty and had been the loudest all night. “If the students in Beijing can set up headquarters, why can't workers?”

So the name was settled, Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters. The question left was who would lead it.

Huang Jinhai sat by the window and said nothing. Someone looked at you. You were a cadre in the security section of No. 17 State Cotton Mill, a Party member, a former soldier, thirty-one years old. Everyone there had heard about the big-character poster you put up at the mill and your trip to Beijing.

Disputed How Wang Hongwen became the leader. Xu Jingxian, “Ten Years a Dream” (《十年一梦》), says he proposed “laying out qualifications” and used his record as Party member, cadre, and former soldier to beat Pan Guoping. Rebel memoirs tend to treat it as the natural result of his record.

191: You sat in the center of the rostrum.
192: Pan Guoping was the rally's executive chair. You sat one row behind him, off to the side.
193: Today it was Pan Guoping's turn to chair. You had agreed beforehand that nobody would decide anything alone.
194:
Culture Square was the largest indoor hall in Shanghai, with seats for 20,000. You had expected a few thousand. Before noon the aisles and all eight doorways were packed with people standing. The red armbands had been made overnight two days before. On some the characters were still wet and had rubbed red onto padded jackets.

⟦0⟧

Everyone was waiting for municipal Party secretary Cao Diqiu. You had invited him beforehand to come and publicly recognize the Workers' General Headquarters as a legitimate revolutionary organization. The rally was set for twelve. You waited until one, then two. He did not come. Backstage someone passed on a remark of his in a low voice. He had said the dregs of society had all come out for today's rally, and attending would be a mistake. Nobody knew if it was true. The person passing it on made it sound real.

A little after two, the rally began anyway. Pan Guoping read the “Declaration.” Before he finished, a young woman in her twenties rushed up from the left of the stage, grabbed the microphone, and said Pan Guoping was a political pickpocket and no worker at all. More than a hundred people pushed toward the stage after her. People from the glass machinery plant rushed up too and said Pan Guoping was a demobilized soldier and a worker at their plant. The stage was chaos. Huang Jinhai gathered a dozen or so men and formed a ring around ⟦1⟧. A tall man with a Tianjin accent jumped up from below and led the shout of “Long live Chairman Mao.” Nobody dared not join that slogan, and the hall settled.

Jiang Zhoufa from the railway loading machinery plant went up to denounce the kangaroo court at his plant. Halfway through he was crying too hard to go on, and Xie Pengfei from the same plant went up and finished for him.

The Municipal Party Committee sent Zhang Wenbao, a deputy head of the Municipal Organization Department. The crowd demanded he speak. He said, I cannot represent the Municipal Party Committee, and I cannot take a position. The crowd jeered.

A light rain began. The people outside stood in the cold wind, and none would leave. A Red Guard came up onto the stage and said, if the Municipal Party Committee won't take a position, nobody can go home. If we break up now, everyone gets punished when they go back. Everyone on the stage was looking at you and the other leaders.
197: “If Cao Diqiu won't come, we go to him. Everyone to 33 West Yan'an Road. We petition at the Municipal Party Committee gate.”

202: November 9　Incited workers to abandon their production posts, force their way north, and disrupt the railway.

205:
History The rally was set for 12:00 but was delayed until after 2:00 p.m. because Cao Diqiu did not arrive. While Pan Guoping was reading the “Declaration,” someone came on stage and called him a “political pickpocket,” setting off a disturbance. Huang Jinhai organized a dozen or so people to guard the rostrum, and Zhang Baolin of the foundation company led a slogan that calmed things. Jiang Zhoufa of the railway loading machinery plant broke down crying during his denunciation, and Xie Pengfei finished for him. Zhang Wenbao, deputy head of the Municipal Organization Department, said, “I cannot represent the Municipal Party Committee.” See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 4. Wang Rui, citing “The Anting Storm” (《安亭风暴》) in “Workers' Rebel News” (《工人造反报》), May 19, 1967, says the hall was stormed twice by the opposing faction.

Disputed Cao Diqiu's remark, “the dregs of society have all come out, and if I attend I'll be making a mistake,” is quoted by Wang Rui as hearsay. Its source has not been verified.

History Historically, Wang Hongwen took the microphone and announced that “all participants will go together to petition the Municipal Party Committee.” This is the basis for the first option. The call to go to Beijing was shouted by a Red Guard after midnight outside the Sino-Soviet Friendship Building, according to Huang Jinhai's memoir.

Fiction Going home after the rally is a game branch.
208:
You got to the mill at 6:30. The security section door was locked, and the key was in your pocket.

At lunch in the canteen, the loudspeaker said nothing about it, but people were talking. Before dawn about 2,000 people had boarded a train at North Station. The train never reached Beijing. It stopped at a small station past Jiading called Anting. Someone had stopped trains on the line, and the Shanghai-Nanjing line was cut.

Someone asked you, “Comrade Wang, weren't you at Culture Square yesterday too?”

You said you had come back to work. The man looked at you for a while, then left with his lunch box.

Everything after that you learned from the newspapers. The names you knew appeared on the front page one by one, then disappeared from it one by one. In October 1976 the workshop loudspeaker read out a list of names. Yours was not among them.

In 1977, during the mill's investigation, someone dug up your name on the sign-in sheet from Culture Square. You wrote three self-criticisms. In the 1990s, when the mill was restructured, you were in your fifties. You took a buyout of your years of service and went home.

You wake. In Qincheng the light stays on all night. This time you dreamed of another man's life.
209:
History did not stop for lack of you. On November 10, more than 2,000 people got off the train at Anting. On the 13th, Zhang Chunqiao signed at Culture Square, with Pan Guoping standing beside him as he signed. The heads of the Workers' General Headquarters were Pan Guoping and a few other Standing Committee members. None of them came from the ranks of Party cadres.

Later Zhang Chunqiao needed a worker he could rely on in Shanghai, and he searched for a long time. Kangping Road, the January Storm, and Shanghai Diesel Liansi all happened just the same. Only the people on the stage were different. On National Day 1968, the Chairman did not ask on Tiananmen who Wang Hongwen was. At the Tenth Party Congress in 1973, there was no worker on the list of Vice Chairmen. The Chairman's idea of picking a successor from among the workers came up a few times and went nowhere.

On October 6, 1976, three people were arrested at Huairen Hall. That Week in Shanghai still set up its liaison posts, and still took them down. In the dock of the Special Court in 1981, the “Jiang Qing counterrevolutionary clique” was just four people, Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Chen Boda.
210: Fiction The back-to-the-mill route is a game branch. It asks whether history happens the same way after one person steps out, and whether the person who steps out can really get free.
211: Night of November 9 to noon of November 10, 1966
212: West Yan'an Road · North Station · Anting Station
213: You shouted to go to Beijing, and the hall shouted with you. But once the crowd left Culture Square, it surged toward the Municipal Party Committee first. Everyone wanted to get a word out of them first.
214: You took the microphone and announced that everyone would go to petition the Municipal Party Committee. Stay together, you said, and follow instructions.
215: Everyone in the car was looking at you.
216: Pan Guoping was not on this train. Someone said he had squeezed onto the first one, which went toward Nanjing. Everyone in the car was looking at you.
217:
⟦0⟧

It was cold and drizzling, and many people dropped away on the way. More than 2,000 stood in front of the Municipal Party Committee building at 33 West Yan'an Road. They waited until after six, and Cao Diqiu did not come out. The loudspeaker said Cao Diqiu would receive everyone at the Sino-Soviet Friendship Building. The crowd surged over there and lost its ranks. Only a little over 1,000 arrived, and the café door stayed shut. You stood outside until two in the morning. The man who came out was Zhang Qi from the city's trade union federation. He said, well, this organization is not in the Sixteen Points.

A Red Guard raised a megaphone and shouted, we're going to Beijing, we're going to see Chairman Mao. Everyone took up the shout at once. The crowd poured toward North Station in a rush, and you could not tell who was leading.

The first train pulled out. Later you heard it went all the way to Nanjing before it was held. At seven in the morning, more than 2,000 of you crammed onto express No. 65. Some had brought two steamed buns. Some had brought nothing. At Nanxiang the station ordered everyone off and onto slow train No. 602. The slow train ran for a while. At 8:17 it turned onto a siding at Anting Station, stopped beside a coal yard used for loading and unloading, and did not move again.

⟦1⟧

The station already had boiled water and bread ready. Someone said these things had been set out the day before. The Municipal Party Committee had planned all along to hold you here.

The cars held people from seventy or eighty work units. One factory had sent more than 300. From the rest came a few or a dozen each. Someone said quietly, when I go back I'll be the only one in my factory, they'll gang up on me and finish me. From today, everyone who got on this train was a person who had “left their post and disrupted the railway.” The only thing left that could make the Center hear them was the railway itself.

⟦2⟧

In the morning, some people ran out to the main line and waved their caps, then took off their padded jackets and waved those. The driver of an oncoming passenger train thought something had happened ahead and braked hard. Once the train had stopped, people climbed onto the tracks one by one. Some stood, some sat, some lay down. Later people called it lying on the tracks to stop trains.

This stretch at Anting was single track. With one train stopped here, nothing could pass in either direction. Just after noon, an express heading north came along and was stopped the same way. Someone said there were foreign guests on board.

The November wind blew in off the fields. Your hands were in your jacket pockets, and you felt the armband with the name of the Workers' General Headquarters on it. The people on that express were ordinary folk, just like you.
218: Be the first to step down onto the tracks.
219: Step down and stand among the people on the tracks.

221: November 10　Lay on the tracks at Anting Station to stop trains, cutting the Shanghai-Nanjing line for more than 30 hours.
222: Wait until the people ahead have gone down, then follow.
223: November 10　Kept up the struggle at Anting Station.
224: Stay on the platform and urge people not to stop the trains.
225: November 10　At Anting Station, held reservations about stopping trains.
227:
History After the rally, more than 2,000 people went to petition at the Municipal Party Committee at 33 West Yan'an Road. After waiting until past six, they were directed to the Sino-Soviet Friendship Building, by which time about 1,000 remained. After midnight Zhang Qi of the city's trade union federation came out and said, “well, this organization is not in the Sixteen Points.” A Red Guard shouted to go to Beijing, and the crowd surged toward North Station on its own. See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 4. Wang Rui, citing “The Anting Storm” (《安亭风暴》), gives the place as the Friendship Cinema (inside the Sino-Soviet Friendship Building).

History At 7:00 on the 10th, more than 2,000 people boarded express No. 65, changed to slow train No. 602 at Nanxiang, and were stopped at Anting at 8:17. Anting Station had been told in advance by the Municipal Party Committee to prepare food and boiled water. The stretch at Anting was single track. The first train went to Nanjing and was held there (Huang Jinhai records it as No. 626). See Wang Rui, “Rethinking and Re-researching the ‘Anting Incident’” (《“安亭事件”的再认识和再研究》). Those stranded came from seventy or eighty work units and feared punishment when they returned. See Wang Rui, citing the telephone report that Zhen Wenjun, the Central Cultural Revolution Group's liaison in Shanghai, made to Zhou Enlai on the 12th.

Disputed How the trains were stopped. Ye Yonglie calls it “stopping trains by lying on the tracks.” People by the line waved caps and clothes, the driver braked hard, and only then did people go onto the tracks. They first stopped passenger train No. 648, then at 12:02 express No. 14. A 1979 document from the Shanghai Railway Sub-bureau dispatch office says traffic was cut for 31 hours 34 minutes. Ye Yonglie says No. 14 was held for 20 hours 21 minutes. Huang Jinhai holds that No. 648 stopped for only twenty-odd minutes and that the long hold of No. 14 was invented afterward. Ye Changming recalls that No. 14 “stopped a bit longer and then also left.” At his trial in 1980, Wang Hongwen said, “Although I did not favor their stopping the trains, and I did work on them, the main responsibility is still mine, because I was the head.” The Special Court's verdict does not mention Anting. See Wang Rui's article and Huang Jinhai, ch. 4.

Design Note that the third option also leaves a line in the 1977 dossier.
231:
You did not go down. You stood at the edge of the platform and shouted to the people on the tracks. The train has been stopped, you said, so Beijing knows. You can come back up now.

The people on the tracks turned to look at you. Someone recognized you and said, isn't that Wang Hongwen from No. 17 State Cotton Mill? Someone else said, he's from the security section, and the security section just keeps the door for the Party committee.

More and more people gathered on the platform. Some got off the train to relieve themselves, some to see what had happened up ahead. Passengers from the express stood in the doorways holding string bags, afraid to get off. A woman holding a child asked you when the train would leave. You had no answer.

You knew the place where you stood was very narrow. One step forward were the people on the tracks. One step back were the people on the train. There was a heavy sentence in your throat.
232: “You've stopped a trainload of ordinary people. You're holding them hostage.”
233: November 10　Quarreled with the crowd stopping trains at Anting Station.
235: Swallow the words. You back away to a pillar on the platform and watch.
236:
History Questioned on June 5, 1980, Wang Hongwen said, “Although I did not favor their stopping the trains, and I did work on them, the main responsibility is still mine, because I was the head.” See Wang Rui's article, citing Wang Nianyi, “Some Materials on the ‘Anting Incident’” (《关于“安亭事件”的一些资料》), in “Party History Research Materials” (《党史研究资料》), 2002, no. 4. This option is therefore not wholly fiction. It is close to the account Wang Hongwen later gave of himself.

Fiction The talk on the platform and the woman with the child are the game's invention. Huang Jinhai was not at Anting that day. He arrived only on the evening of the 11th.
240:
The moment you said it, the platform went quiet.

Then the crowd surged toward you all at once. Nobody pushed you on purpose. The people behind pressed forward, and the people in front could not keep their footing. You stepped back, your heel found nothing, and you fell off the edge of the platform. The back of your head struck the gravel of the embankment.

The last thing you remember is someone's padded cotton shoe, with a patch of blue cloth sewn on the side.

You woke in the hospital in Jiading County, your head wrapped in gauze and your left leg in a cast. The nurse said railway workers had brought you in. You asked if the train had left. She said yes, long ago.

On November 13, the loudspeaker in the ward announced that Comrade Zhang Chunqiao had signed at Culture Square, and the Workers' General Headquarters was a legitimate revolutionary organization. The names read out included Pan Guoping and others. Yours was not among them.

By the time you left the hospital it was December. People at the mill said that while you were in the hospital, someone from the Workers' General Headquarters came to see you once and left a kilo of apples.
241:
The Workers' General Headquarters was founded without you. When Zhang Chunqiao signed on November 13, the man standing beside him was Pan Guoping. On the 14th, the spearhead squad at Kunshan Middle School beat a different headquarters member who had gone to talk people round.

Afterward things went on much as before. Kangping Road, the January Storm, the Shanghai People's Commune, Shanghai Diesel Liansi, not one was missing. Every list was simply one name short. Zhang Chunqiao needed a worker at his side and chose someone else. That man became a Central Committee member in 1969, was sent to Beijing to study in 1971, and in 1973 failed to become Vice Chairman. The Chairman said he was too soft.

In October 1976, three people were arrested at Huairen Hall. You were in the No. 17 Mill security section listening to the radio. When you heard the words “Gang of Four,” you paused and counted. There were only three.

Your leg aches when it rains. In the 1990s the mill cut back its spindles. You were in your fifties, and you retired.

248: Afterward　This name does not appear on the Workers' General Headquarters roster.
250:
FictionNo injury on the platform is recorded in the sources. But with 2,000 people crowded into a small station and a coal yard, the risk of being hurt in the crush was real.

History Historically the Workers' General Headquarters was recognized on November 13, and that would have happened without Wang Hongwen present. This is what the game calls the inertia of history.
251: On an express held at Anting
253:
Point of view shift. You are now Zhou Yue'e, forty-one, a machine tender at one of the state cotton mills. Fictional character

You had taken three days' leave to go to Nanjing. Your mother was in the hospital. You got the ticket through someone you knew, a hard seat on express No. 14. The train braked hard, your string bag fell from the luggage rack, and apples rolled all over the floor. After it stopped, no one came to say why. Someone in a car up front said there were foreigners on board, and the train police had all gone over there.

⟦0⟧

Across from you sat Old Lu from your mill, a maintenance fitter and longtime Party member who later joined the Scarlet Guards. His name was Lu Genbao. He was a few years younger than you, and whenever a machine broke down in the workshop, people went to him. He looked out the window, his face dark. “Look at that. That's the rebels for you. They won't even let the train run. Every day the machines stand idle, how much cloth do we lose?”

You looked out too. A crowd stood on the tracks, stamping their feet against the cold. ⟦1⟧ Someone was pushing leaflets in through the window. They said the workers of Shanghai were being oppressed, please tell the whole country. You knew one of the people on the tracks. He was from the next workshop. Last year he was named an advanced worker, and it was your own team that put him forward.

Old Lu said these people had all been stirred up by bad elements, and the mill would look into them properly when they got back. As he said it he kept gripping his work ID, very tight. You said nothing. You were thinking about Nanjing, and whether anyone had brought your mother her meals today.

You picked up seven apples. Two more had rolled under other people's seats, and you didn't ask for them. When it was nearly dark, you got off the train after all, walked along the sleepers to the man you knew, and asked him why they were doing this. He said he didn't know how long they would hold the train either. Then he said, sorry, sister. He took off his padded cap and offered it to you. You didn't take it. Back in the car, Old Lu looked at you and said nothing. He pushed his army greatcoat over toward you.
254: There was another man on the platform. He had been arguing loudly with the people on the tracks. Now he had stopped, and stood alone, leaning against a pillar.
256:
Fiction Zhou Yue'e and Old Lu (Lu Genbao) are composite characters. They are there so that conservatives and ordinary passengers are present in the scene. Many Scarlet Guard members were Party or Youth League members and model workers who sincerely believed they were defending the Party committees and production. The passengers who were held up were simply people caught in it.

History The 1979 document from the Shanghai Railway Sub-bureau dispatch office says the No. 14 Shanghai-Beijing express “carried foreign guests.” On those stopping the trains passing leaflets to passengers, see Huang Jinhai's memoir (paraphrased, from accounts by members at his mill). How long No. 14 was held is disputed. See the previous source note.
259:
You spent the night by the coal yard. There was no heat in the cars. Some people pulled the cloth covers off the seats to cover themselves. Some fainted from hunger and stale air. The Municipal Party Committee sent people with bread, but you had to sign to get it, and someone went car to car with a bread receipt. Many refused it. They said, eat the Municipal Party Committee's bread and you'll never be able to explain yourself. ⟦0⟧ Rebels from some factories brought their own steamed buns and rice porridge, and people fought to get some.

After dark, Han Zheyi, secretary of the East China Bureau, came. He stood at a car door and said everyone had been wronged, and he apologized on behalf of the organization. He said a special express could take everyone to Beijing. Someone asked for his signature as a keepsake, and he wrote one line in a notebook, “Wishing everyone success going north.” Someone in the car cried.

But the next day, what came was a telegram from Beijing. First people from the Municipal Party Committee went car to car handing it out as a leaflet. Then the station loudspeaker read it too.

⟦1⟧

An old master worker said, listen, the Center still sees us as workers. The man next to him said, listen again, it only talks about production, not revolution. Someone else said the telegram was forged by the Municipal Party Committee, and Chen Boda would never say such a thing. The Red Guards and the cadres handing out leaflets started arguing on the spot.

Toward evening, Huang Jinhai of No. 31 State Cotton Mill arrived in a borrowed vehicle and settled more than a hundred people from his mill into one of the cars. He searched everywhere for people from headquarters and found none.

After dark word came through. Zhang Chunqiao of the Central Cultural Revolution Group had flown into Shanghai.
260: When it was your turn, the man looked at you and said, the one from the platform has to eat too.
262: In the middle of the night, someone came for you. Zhang Chunqiao was waiting at a factory in the town.
263:
History The Municipal Party Committee sent bread, and most people refused it. Rebels from some factories brought steamed buns and rice porridge. Some people fainted in the cars. Han Zheyi, secretary of the East China Bureau, came to Anting, apologized for the wrongs people had suffered, agreed to send a special express to take them to Beijing, and on request signed and wrote “Wishing everyone success going north.” Chen Boda's telegram was then distributed as a leaflet, and some thought the Municipal Party Committee had forged it. See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 4. Ye Changming recalls that Han Zheyi came to Anting on the evening of the 10th with a vice mayor.

History Chen Boda's telegram stressed “grasp revolution, promote production.” It told the workers to “stay at your production posts and fulfill the state plan,” and said “minor principles obey major principles, and doing production well is the major principle.” The workers' complaint was that it “only talks about production, not revolution.” See Wang Rui's article. Wang Rui argues the telegram in fact spoke for the Politburo Standing Committee headed by Zhou Enlai.

History Ye Yonglie says he once found a signed list of bread receipts from Anting dated November 10, 1966. See Sina, “A Surprise from a Chance Lead” (《偶然线索带来的惊异》).

Fiction The old master worker's words and the details of the signing are the game's invention.
264: Late night of November 11 to early morning of November 12, 1966
265: Anting · A room at the Radio Special Machinery Plant
267: Zhang Chunqiao's eyes swept across the faces and stopped on you. You were the head of the Workers' General Headquarters, and he knew it.
268: Zhang Chunqiao shook hands with Pan Guoping first, and only then turned to look at you.
269: As you came in, someone behind you said, “The one from the platform.” Everyone in the room heard it.
270:
Zhang Chunqiao had arrived in Shanghai by special plane after nine in the evening. Later you heard that the moment he got off the plane he phoned Chen Boda in Beijing to ask whether to go to the Municipal Party Committee first or to the masses first. Chen Boda said, the masses first. He did not go into the city. He came straight to Anting by car.

One lamp was lit in the room, and the ashtray filled fast. Nine worker representatives had come to talk, among them you, Pan Guoping, back from Nanjing, and Xie Pengfei. There were also two Red Guards, Bao Pao of the Beijing Third Headquarters and Jiang Bixiong of the Shanghai Bombard Headquarters.

⟦0⟧

⟦1⟧

He was not tall, wore glasses, and spoke slowly, one sentence at a time. He opened in a scolding tone. The workers should go back to Shanghai and make revolution where they were, he said, and other questions could be discussed later. He took a sheet of paper from his pocket and said, this is the original draft of the telegram in Comrade Chen Boda's own hand. Have a look.

Bao Pao was the first to push back. “In Beijing you back the Red Guards, and in Shanghai you come to crush the workers?”

Pan Guoping spoke next. He talked about Culture Square, about Cao Diqiu not coming, about the people put through kangaroo courts. He spoke fast and sometimes pounded the table. Zhang Chunqiao did not interrupt. He took notes in his notebook and gave no ground. He would not say whether Anting was a revolutionary action.

Of the nine, three said they could go back. Six said they would not, and would walk to Beijing if they had to. It was nearly dawn, and everyone in the room had looked at you at least once.
271: You sat to one side, smoking one cigarette after another, and listened to Little Pan.
272: November 12　At the Anting negotiations, assisted Comrade Pan Guoping in talks with the representative of the Center.
273: November 12　Took part in the Anting negotiations.
274: “Comrade Chunqiao, I support your view. The Workers' General Headquarters will withdraw to Shanghai. But there are a few questions I need you to take a position on.”
275: You told people on the platform not to stop the trains. At this table, that line is not yours to say.
276: November 12　Reached agreement with Comrade Zhang Chunqiao that the Workers' General Headquarters would withdraw to Shanghai.
277: November 12　Colluded and bargained with Zhang Chunqiao, paving the way to usurp the Party and carry out a power seizure.
278: “Until the Workers' General Headquarters is recognized, we don't retreat one step. If the trains won't run, we walk to Beijing.”
279: Someone who stood on the platform cannot say this.
280: November 12　Insisted that the Center recognize the Workers' General Headquarters and led some workers to continue north.
281: November 12　Refused to carry out instructions from the Center and kept inciting workers to go north.
282: “The telegram is right. Whoever wants to go back, come with me first.”
283: November 12　Answered the Center's call and led some workers back to Shanghai.
284: November 12　Returned to Shanghai in the middle and late stage of the Anting Incident.
285:
History Zhang Chunqiao arrived in Shanghai after 9 p.m. on the 11th and first phoned Chen Boda to ask “whether to go first to the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee, or first to the masses.” Chen answered, “first to the masses.” He went to Anting and negotiated with nine worker representatives. “Of the 9, 3 agreed to persuade the workers to return to Shanghai, 6 did not. The talks went on until dawn without agreement, and they insisted on walking to Beijing.” See Wang Rui, citing Zhen Wenjun's telephone report to Zhou Enlai on the afternoon of the 12th. The talks were held at the Anting Radio Special Machinery Plant. Present were Wang Hongwen, Pan Guoping (back from Nanjing), and the Red Guards Bao Pao and Jiang Bixiong. Zhang Chunqiao “wore away at it all night ... and basically gave no ground.” See Huang Jinhai, ch. 4. Bao Pao confronting Zhang Chunqiao to his face is from Xie Pengfei's recollection (as retold by RFA).

Disputed Whether Wang Hongwen spoke during the talks. RFA, citing Ye Yonglie, “Biography of Wang Hongwen” (《王洪文传》), says Pan Guoping did most of the talking and Wang Hongwen “sat to one side, smoking constantly, listening intently, saying nothing.” In “Figures of Zhongnanhai” (《中南海人物春秋》), Ye Yonglie writes instead that Wang Hongwen first voiced support and then raised conditions. The first option follows the former account, the second the latter. Huang Jinhai did not take part in the talks and cannot confirm either.

Disputed Who sent Zhang Chunqiao. Drawing on accounts by Wang Li and Chen Boda, Wang Rui holds that he was sent by the Politburo Standing Committee headed by Zhou Enlai, with Li Fuchun briefing him on the mission, and that Zhang Chunqiao privately met Jiang Qing before leaving.
289: At dawn, Zhang Chunqiao agreed to come out to the coal yard and meet everyone. He said, after that, everyone goes back to Shanghai. You said yes.
290: At dawn you came out of that room and went car by car, asking who was willing to go back first.
291: At dawn Pan Guoping came out of that room and said Zhang Chunqiao would come out to the coal yard to meet everyone.
292:
⟦0⟧

In the morning a fine drizzle began. Zhang Chunqiao stood on a big truck with a loudspeaker mounted on it, and ⟦1⟧ stood beside him. As soon as the truck drove into the coal yard, people packed in around it on all sides.

Someone behind him was holding an umbrella over him. A voice from below shouted, put the umbrella away. He turned and said a few words. The umbrella was closed, and he stood in the rain with everyone else.

Then came the denunciations. No one organized them. One after another, people climbed onto the truck's hood and wheel guards and talked about the work teams, the black materials, being locked up, beaten, having wages docked. One woman worker fainted by the wheels in the middle of speaking, and several people carried her out. It went on like this until one or two in the afternoon, five or six hours, and Zhang Chunqiao stood on the truck listening the whole time.

Then the Red Guards shouted for him to take a position. He said the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee had carried out a wrong line. Your actions had been forced on you by the Municipal Party Committee. Until your problems were solved, he would not go back to Beijing. He hoped everyone would go back first and solve the problems in the city.

Some said he was a liar trying to trick everyone into going back. About 500 people said that whatever he said, they would walk to Beijing if they had to.

Huang Jinhai pushed his way over to you. People could go back, he said, but not straight to their units. With just a few people from each factory, they'd be punished once they got there. He said he would ask Zhang Chunqiao for vehicles and take everyone to Culture Square to wait together, and they would go back to their factories only once the problems were solved.

The hundred-odd people from No. 17 Mill gathered around you, waiting for you to speak.
